questions.stem: A 48 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 9 years has numbness and tingling in both feet. He rarely takes his medicines and misses clinic appointments. He does not drink alcohol. He has symmetrical loss of light touch to the ankles. His recent HbA1c results have all been above 90 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely factor contributing to his condition?
questions.e: Chronic hyperglycaemia from poor control is the key risk factor, with duration of diabetes, smoking and obesity.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely factor contributing to his condition?
Persistently high HbA1c.

elim: Not a cause of neuropathy.
He is male, and sex is not a listed risk factor.
Protective, not a risk factor.
Not the main driver of diabetic neuropathy.

steps.x: C: Poor glycaemic control. Risk factors: poor control, long duration, smoking, obesity.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with type 2 diabetes for 22 years has had three falls at night when walking to the bathroom in the dark. She feels her feet are 'like cotton wool'. Romberg's test is positive. Joint position sense is absent at the great toes and ankle reflexes are absent. Her lying and standing BP are 138/80 and 134/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her falls?
questions.e: Loss of proprioception from diabetic neuropathy causes sensory ataxia, worse in the dark (positive Romberg).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her falls?
Sensory ataxia with absent proprioception.

elim: Romberg is negative in cerebellar ataxia, and sensation would be normal.
Causes gait apraxia with incontinence and confusion, not sensory loss.
No tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia.
Her standing BP barely falls.

steps.x: B: Diabetic sensory neuropathy. Diabetic neuropathy causes unsteadiness through lost proprioception.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 15 years has 1 year of tingling in both feet. He has symmetrical loss of light touch to the mid-shin and reduced vibration sense at both great toes. Foot pulses are present and power is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
o: Brisk knee reflexes with upgoing plantars
questions.e: Distal symmetrical neuropathy reduces or abolishes the ankle reflexes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?

clues: symmetrical loss of light touch to the mid-shin
steps.x: A distal symmetrical sensory neuropathy.

elim: Upper motor neurone signs suggest cord disease such as B12 deficiency.
A sign of parkinsonism.
Suggests motor neurone disease.
Suggests myopathy; power is normal.

steps.x: E: Reduced ankle reflexes. Diabetic neuropathy: lost vibration, proprioception and light touch, reduced ankle reflexes.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 25 years first noticed numbness in his toes 6 years ago. It has slowly crept up to his knees and he now has tingling in his fingertips. Examination shows symmetrical reduced sensation in both legs to the knees and in both hands to the wrists.
questions.q: Which pattern of sensory loss is he most likely to have?
questions.e: Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy starts in the feet and ascends, then the hands: a glove and stocking pattern.

steps.x: The question asks: Which pattern of sensory loss is he most likely to have?

clues: slowly crept up to his knees
steps.x: Bilateral, distal, ascending.

elim: A single root lesion; unilateral.
One side of the body; a central lesion.
Cauda equina syndrome.
Spinal cord lesion.

steps.x: B: Glove and stocking distribution. Diabetic neuropathy = glove and stocking, feet first.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with type 1 diabetes for 35 years has a weak urinary stream and dribbling. He does not feel when his bladder is full. A bladder scan shows a post-void residual of 600 mL. Digital rectal examination shows a small, smooth prostate. Perianal sensation and anal tone are normal and he has no back pain. He also has erectile dysfunction.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his urinary symptoms?
questions.e: Autonomic neuropathy causes a large, insensate bladder with retention and erectile dysfunction.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his urinary symptoms?

clues: does not feel when his bladder is full
steps.x: Painless retention with ED in long-standing diabetes.

elim: The prostate is small and smooth.
No back pain; perianal sensation and anal tone are normal.
Causes urgency, not a large painless residual.
No history of trauma or infection; does not explain loss of bladder sensation.

steps.x: D: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy. Autonomic neuropathy: postural hypotension, gastroparesis, ED, bladder dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has 3 months of tingling in her right thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night and improves when she shakes her hand. She has wasting of the thenar eminence. Sensation in her feet and little finger is normal. Tinel's test at the wrist is positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diabetes causes focal entrapment neuropathies such as carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: Tinel's test at the wrist is positive
steps.x: A single nerve in the median distribution.

elim: Affects the little finger and medial hand.
Would be bilateral and start in the feet.
Colour change with cold, no wasting.
Affects the little finger, which is normal.

steps.x: C: Median nerve entrapment neuropathy. Focal diabetic neuropathy: cranial nerve palsies or entrapment.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with type 2 diabetes and neuropathy has a painless ulcer under the head of his right first metatarsal. It has a punched-out base surrounded by thick callus. His foot is warm and the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily felt. He cannot feel a 10 g monofilament on either foot.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A painless ulcer with callus over a pressure point in a warm, pulsed, insensate foot is neuropathic.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Pressure-point ulcer, sensation lost, pulses present.

elim: Pulses are present and the foot is warm; arterial ulcers are painful.
A squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic scar.
Painful, with violaceous undermined edges.
Found over the gaiter area, not the plantar surface.

steps.x: C: Neuropathic ulcer. Lost protective sensation leads to neuropathic ulceration at pressure points.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with type 2 diabetes for 18 years comes to clinic because her daughter noticed blood on her sock. A drawing pin is found embedded in the sole of her left foot; she thinks it has been there for about a week. She had no pain. Her foot pulses are present and her eyesight is good.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason the injury went unnoticed?
questions.e: Neuropathy removes protective sensation, so trauma goes unnoticed and leads to ulceration.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely reason the injury went unnoticed?
A painless penetrating injury.

elim: Dry skin does not stop pain being felt.
Pulses are present; ischaemia does not abolish pain.
Her eyesight is good, and she would still feel it.
Does not cause loss of sensation.

steps.x: B: Loss of protective sensation. Lost protective sensation = unnoticed trauma and ulceration.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 14 years has 3 days of horizontal double vision that is worse when he looks to the left. His left eye cannot move outwards beyond the midline. Pupils, eyelids and other eye movements are normal. He has no headache, weakness or fatigue on repeated movements.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Failure of abduction of one eye is a sixth nerve palsy, a diabetic cranial mononeuropathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: cannot move outwards beyond the midline
Pupils, eyelids and other eye movements are normal
steps.x: Isolated failure of abduction.

elim: Causes failure of adduction, not abduction.
Fatigable, with ptosis; not described.
Causes a third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil.
Causes proptosis and restricted upgaze.

steps.x: A: Diabetic abducens nerve palsy. Diabetes causes cranial nerve mononeuropathies (III, VI).

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 32 years feels faint whenever she gets out of bed. She takes no antihypertensive drugs and drinks 2 litres of fluid a day. Her lying BP and pulse are recorded, then repeated after 3 minutes standing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on standing?
o: No change in BP or pulse rate
Rise in pulse rate of 40 bpm with stable BP
Systolic fall of 30 mmHg with a pulse rise of 30 bpm
Systolic fall of 30 mmHg with no rise in pulse rate
questions.e: Autonomic neuropathy causes postural hypotension; the failed sympathetic response means the pulse does not rise.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on standing?
Long-standing diabetes, no drug cause.

elim: Would not explain her symptoms.
Postural tachycardia syndrome.
A compensatory tachycardia suggests hypovolaemia; autonomic failure blunts this.
Not a recognised pattern.

steps.x: D: Systolic fall of 30 mmHg with no rise in pulse rate. Autonomic neuropathy: postural hypotension with a fixed heart rate.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with type 1 diabetes since childhood has 6 months of burning and prickling pain in both feet, worse at night, and her bedsheets feel painful on her toes. She does not drink alcohol. She has symmetrical loss of pinprick to the ankles. Foot pulses are present.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Burning, night-time, ascending symmetrical pain with allodynia in a patient with poorly controlled diabetes is diabetic neuropathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Night pain, allodynia, symmetrical distal loss.

elim: She does not drink alcohol.
Acute ascending weakness over days, not 6 months of pain.
Thyroid function is normal.
B12 is normal.

steps.x: B: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Painful distal symmetrical neuropathy in diabetes, after excluding B12, thyroid and alcohol.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with type 2 diabetes attends his annual diabetic foot review. He has no symptoms. His skin is intact and his foot pulses are present. The nurse wants a quick bedside test to see whether he has lost protective sensation, which would put him at higher risk of ulceration.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate test?
questions.e: Diabetic neuropathy is a clinical diagnosis; the 10 g monofilament detects loss of protective sensation at the foot review.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate test?
A clinical bedside test is needed.

elim: Assesses arterial disease, not sensation.
Reserved for uncertain diagnoses.
Does not assess sensation.
Not a screening test.

steps.x: A: 10 g monofilament testing. Diagnosis is clinical: monofilament and tuning fork at the bedside.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has tingling in both feet. Her GP finds symmetrical loss of light touch to the ankles. Before deciding the diagnosis, the GP wants to test the sensory modality that is often lost earliest in diabetic neuropathy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate bedside test?
o: 128 Hz tuning fork on the great toe
questions.e: Loss of vibration sense at the great toe, tested with a 128 Hz tuning fork, is an early sign.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate bedside test?
Early loss is vibration sense, distally.

elim: Tests cerebellar function.
Proximal; not where early loss occurs.
Romberg needs the eyes closed and tests proprioception.
Not a standard early test in the feet.

steps.x: A: 128 Hz tuning fork on the great toe. Clinical diagnosis: vibration (tuning fork), proprioception, light touch, ankle reflexes.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with type 2 diabetes has been diagnosed with peripheral neuropathy on examination. His glucose-lowering treatment has been intensified to slow progression. His diabetes nurse wants a single blood test to monitor whether his average glucose control over the past 3 months has improved.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: HbA1c reflects average glycaemia over about 3 months and is checked to assess control.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: average glucose control over the past 3 months
steps.x: A 3-month average is needed.

elim: A single moment, not a 3-month average.
A single moment, not a 3-month average.
Measures insulin production, not control.
Poor marker of control.

steps.x: B: HbA1c. HbA1c assesses glycaemic control; tight control slows neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman with type 2 diabetes for 4 years has 2 months of rapidly worsening weakness and numbness that began in her hands before her feet. Her right hand is weaker than her left. Her HbA1c is 54 mmol/mol, and B12 and thyroid function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: The picture is atypical (rapid, hands first, asymmetrical), so the diagnosis is uncertain and nerve conduction studies are needed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: began in her hands before her feet
steps.x: Atypical features.

elim: Would not explain hand-first, asymmetrical features.
Delays assessment of an atypical neuropathy.
Too slow for a rapidly progressive picture.
Not the next step.

steps.x: B: Nerve conduction studies. Clinical diagnosis normally; nerve conduction studies when uncertain.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with type 2 diabetes and neuropathy has a 10 day history of a hot, swollen left midfoot. He cannot remember any injury. The skin is intact with no ulcer. The left foot is 3°C warmer than the right. His temperature is 36.8°C. CRP is 6 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Suspected Charcot foot needs an urgent foot X-ray first (MRI if the X-ray is normal), per NICE NG19.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
Hot swollen neuropathic foot without infection.

elim: Assesses arterial disease, not the bones.
He is afebrile with a normal CRP.
Not relevant to a foot bone process.
His neuropathy is already known.

steps.x: E: Plain X-ray of the foot. Suspected Charcot: X-ray first, offload, refer to the foot team.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has burning pain in both feet that keeps her awake. Examination confirms painful distal symmetrical neuropathy. She has primary open-angle glaucoma treated with latanoprost eye drops. She has no liver disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her pain?
questions.e: Duloxetine is a safe, effective choice when amitriptyline is contraindicated, as in glaucoma or BPH.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her pain?
Neuropathic pain but amitriptyline is contraindicated.

elim: Contraindicated in primary open-angle glaucoma.
Not recommended for neuropathic pain.
Ineffective for neuropathic pain.
Not recommended for chronic neuropathic pain.

steps.x: C: Duloxetine. Amitriptyline first unless glaucoma or BPH; then duloxetine.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has painful diabetic neuropathy. He has taken gabapentin at the maximum dose for 10 weeks with little benefit. He has no glaucoma or urinary symptoms. He asks whether another tablet could be added to the gabapentin.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase gabapentin above the maximum dose
questions.e: Neuropathic pain drugs are used as monotherapy: stop the failed drug and switch to another.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: maximum dose for 10 weeks with little benefit
steps.x: First drug failed.

elim: Monotherapy is recommended; stop one before starting another.
Monotherapy is recommended.
Unsafe.
Not recommended for chronic neuropathic pain.

steps.x: E: Stop gabapentin and start duloxetine. Monotherapy: switch, do not add.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has painful diabetic neuropathy. She has tried amitriptyline, then duloxetine, then pregabalin, each at an adequate dose for at least 8 weeks, one at a time. Her pain still stops her sleeping and walking. Her HbA1c is 56 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Refer to the pain management clinic
Restart amitriptyline at a lower dose
questions.e: If pain remains uncontrolled despite first and second-line drugs, refer to a pain management clinic.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
All drug options tried in sequence.

elim: Monotherapy is recommended.
Already failed.
Not recommended for neuropathic pain.
Only for short-term rescue, not long-term.

steps.x: B: Refer to the pain management clinic. Uncontrolled neuropathic pain = pain clinic referral.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with type 2 diabetes is found to have early peripheral neuropathy at his annual review. He has mild numbness in his toes but no pain. His HbA1c is 86 mmol/mol on metformin alone. He asks what will most slow the nerve damage.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.e: Tight glucose control slows progression of diabetic neuropathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate intervention?
Poor control; the question is about progression.

elim: Treats neuropathic pain; he has none, and it does not slow progression.
Symptomatic only.
Symptomatic only.
Not effective without deficiency.

steps.x: C: Improve glycaemic control. Glucose control slows progression; painkillers only treat symptoms.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with type 1 diabetes for 28 years has 4 months of bloating, early fullness and vomiting several hours after meals. His glucose readings swing unpredictably. Endoscopy is normal and a gastric emptying study is markedly delayed. Small, low-fat meals have not helped.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Diabetic gastroparesis is treated with the prokinetic metoclopramide after dietary measures.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: gastric emptying study is markedly delayed
Small, low-fat meals have not helped
steps.x: Confirmed gastroparesis.

elim: An antispasmodic; slows gut motility further.
Slows gut motility.
Treats acid, not delayed emptying.
An antiemetic that does not speed gastric emptying.

steps.x: C: Metoclopramide. Gastroparesis in autonomic neuropathy = metoclopramide.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and autonomic neuropathy feels dizzy when she stands up quickly in the morning. Her BP is 136/82 mmHg lying and 112/70 mmHg after 3 minutes standing. She takes metformin only and drinks about 1 litre of fluid a day.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Increase fluid intake and stand up slowly
questions.e: Postural hypotension from autonomic neuropathy is managed first with fluids and mobilisation measures.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
Postural drop with low fluid intake.

elim: Considered only if simple measures fail.
Considered only if simple measures fail.
Would worsen postural hypotension.
Would worsen postural hypotension.

steps.x: B: Increase fluid intake and stand up slowly. Autonomic postural hypotension: fluids and slow mobilisation first.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with type 2 diabetes has reduced sensation to a 10 g monofilament on both feet. His skin is intact, his pulses are present and he has no deformity. He walks barefoot at home and soaks his feet in hot water each night to ease stiffness.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
o: Daily foot checks, podiatry and proper footwear
Walk barefoot to toughen the skin
questions.e: Foot care (daily inspection, podiatry, proper footwear) is essential to prevent ulcers in neuropathic feet.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?

clues: soaks his feet in hot water
steps.x: Insensate feet exposed to injury.

elim: Not part of routine foot care.
Risks unnoticed burns in insensate feet.
No infection; not indicated.
Exposes insensate feet to injury.

steps.x: C: Daily foot checks, podiatry and proper footwear. Neuropathic feet: daily checks, podiatry, good footwear (NICE NG19).

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and neuropathy has a 5 day history of a red, swollen left foot. There is a deep, foul-smelling ulcer over the fifth metatarsal head and redness spreading to the ankle. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 104/64 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Oral flucloxacillin and GP review in 1 week
Same-day admission for IV antibiotics and foot team review
questions.e: Diabetic foot infection with systemic upset is limb-threatening and needs urgent admission and multidisciplinary foot team assessment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Spreading infection with sepsis.

elim: Too slow for a limb-threatening, systemic infection.
Too slow.
She needs urgent admission.
Inadequate for a deep, spreading infection.

steps.x: D: Same-day admission for IV antibiotics and foot team review. Diabetic foot infection is limb-threatening: assess and treat urgently.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with type 1 diabetes has poor glycaemic control for many years and now has numb feet. His doctor explains that in nerves, excess glucose is converted by aldose reductase into a sugar alcohol that cannot easily leave the cell, drawing in water and causing oxidative stress.
questions.q: Which molecule is most likely to accumulate?
questions.e: In the polyol pathway, aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol (then fructose), causing osmotic and oxidative nerve damage.

steps.x: The question asks: Which molecule is most likely to accumulate?
Polyol pathway product of glucose.

elim: Accumulates in galactosaemia.
Stored in liver and muscle; not the polyol product.
Produced in insulin deficiency, not by aldose reductase.
Produced in anaerobic metabolism.

steps.x: E: Sorbitol. Polyol pathway: glucose to sorbitol via aldose reductase.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has sudden painful diplopia. She has left ptosis and her left eye is down and out, but the pupil is normal and reactive. MRI and CT angiography show no aneurysm or mass. She recovers fully over 3 months.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her nerve lesion?
questions.e: Microvascular ischaemia of the vasa nervorum damages the nerve core and spares the outer pupillary fibres.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her nerve lesion?
Pupil-sparing third nerve palsy with normal imaging.

elim: Myasthenia gravis.
Multiple sclerosis; imaging is normal.
Imaging excludes this; would involve the pupil.
Imaging is normal.

steps.x: D: Ischaemia of the vasa nervorum. Diabetic mononeuropathy = microvascular (vasa nervorum) ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 20 years has numbness to the mid-shins but only now notices tingling in his fingertips. A medical student asks why his feet were affected years before his hands, even though all his nerves are exposed to the same blood glucose.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: The feet are cooler than the hands
The hands have more nerve endings
The leg nerves are more myelinated
The nerves to the feet are the longest
questions.e: Longer axons are affected earliest and worst, producing a length-dependent glove and stocking pattern.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation?

clues: feet were affected years before his hands
steps.x: The pattern is length-dependent.

elim: Not the explanation for the distribution.
Pressure explains ulcers, not neuropathy distribution.
Not the reason for the pattern.
Myelination does not explain the pattern.

steps.x: E: The nerves to the feet are the longest. Length-dependent: longest nerves (to the feet) first.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 30 years faints when she stands. Her BP falls from 140/84 mmHg lying to 98/60 mmHg standing with no rise in pulse rate. She is not dehydrated and takes no antihypertensives. Her synacthen test is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her postural hypotension?
questions.e: Damage to unmyelinated autonomic fibres causes sympathetic vasomotor failure, so vessels do not constrict on standing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her postural hypotension?
Failure of the autonomic reflex.

elim: Her synacthen test is normal.
She takes no antihypertensives.
She is not dehydrated, and the pulse would rise.
Causes vasovagal syncope, not a fixed postural drop.

steps.x: D: Sympathetic vasomotor failure. Autonomic neuropathy: sympathetic failure causes postural hypotension.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 26 years has early satiety and vomiting of food eaten the day before. Endoscopy shows retained food with no obstruction. A gastric emptying study is delayed. Her calcium and thyroid function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her symptoms?
o: Autonomic damage to the vagus nerve
questions.e: Autonomic neuropathy damaging vagal fibres causes gastroparesis (delayed emptying).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her symptoms?

clues: vomiting of food eaten the day before
steps.x: Delayed emptying, no blockage.

elim: Endoscopy shows no obstruction.
Causes dyspepsia, not delayed emptying with retained food.
Calcium is normal.
Thyroid function is normal.

steps.x: A: Autonomic damage to the vagus nerve. Gastroparesis = vagal autonomic neuropathy.
